techniques.name: Basic Step
techniques.tagline: The foundation — 6 steps, two sets of 3
techniques.what: The On2 basic step is the heartbeat of NY-style salsa. You step on counts 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, with a natural pause (break) on counts 4 and 8. That gives you exactly 6 steps per 8-count phrase. Leaders step forward on 1, followers step back on 1. If you find yourself taking more than 6 steps, you are losing the count — reset and simplify.

mechanics.action: Step forward (leader) or back (follower) with your left foot
Step in place or shift weight to right foot
Step back with left foot, returning toward center
BREAK — hold, no step, reset your weight
Step back with right foot (leader) or forward (follower)
Step in place or shift weight to left foot
Step forward with right foot, returning toward center
BREAK — hold, no step, reset your weight

arm_styling.action: Arms relaxed at sides or in partner frame; no exaggerated movement
Mirror the opposite side; keep elbows soft and close to body

instructor_quotes: Count 1-2-3-5-6-7 for a basic step. That's 6 steps total. If you're stepping more, you're losing time and the count.
There's a break between each set of 3 counts: 1-2-3 (break) 5-6-7 (break). Use these breaks to reset and stay on time.
Followers: don't change your basic step when the leader starts going back with their left foot. Keep your normal pattern until the lead signals otherwise.

frames.caption: Opening position — dancers face forward, weight centered, ready to begin basic step on count 1
Mid-basic: dancers have shifted weight and are moving through counts 2-3, bodies angled slightly toward mirror
Basic step traveling — all three dancers moving in unison, demonstrating the 5-6-7 half of the phrase

techniques.drill: Stand alone without music. Say '1-2-3-BREAK-5-6-7-BREAK' out loud while stepping. Do this for 2 full minutes until the pause feels natural. Then add music at half speed.
techniques.common_error: Taking 8 steps instead of 6 — students add an extra step on the break counts (4 and 8). If your feet are always moving, you are never resetting. Force yourself to pause and feel the break.

techniques.name: Prep Step
techniques.tagline: Twist right to unlock the left turn
techniques.what: The prep step is the setup move that signals an upcoming turn. Before a left (inside) turn, you twist your body to the right on counts 1-2. This rightward twist 'loads' your body like a spring — when you release on count 3, you naturally unwind into the left turn. Without the prep, the turn feels forced and off-balance. Think of it as a conversation with your body: twist right first, then the left turn becomes effortless.

mechanics.action: Step forward as in basic, but begin rotating your torso to the right
Complete the rightward body twist — hips and shoulders rotate right, loading the turn
Release the twist; this is where the turn initiates — pivot begins here
Complete the turn and return to basic step position

arm_styling.action: Right arm stays close to body; left arm begins to lift slightly to frame the upcoming turn
Arms frame the turn — right hand guides, left hand lifts

instructor_quotes: Before a left turn, twist your body to the right to prepare. This unlocks you from the right twist into the left twist on count 3.
twist on 2
prep for the turn

frames.caption: Pre-prep: neutral stance before the body twist begins — note the upright posture and centered weight

Prep completing — weight shifting as the body unwinds, about to initiate the turn

techniques.drill: Practice the prep step without turning. Step forward, twist right on 2, then just step back on 3 without turning. Feel the coil and release. Do 8 reps, then add the full turn.
techniques.common_error: Skipping the twist entirely and just stepping forward. Without the rightward body rotation on count 2, the left turn has no momentum and you will feel stuck or have to muscle through it.

techniques.name: Inside Turn (Left Turn)
techniques.tagline: Turn on 3, face forward on 6, style with intention
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the left turn or traveling left) is the first turn beginners learn in NY On2. The leader signals the turn through the prep step and arm lift; the follower pivots off their right foot on count 3 and completes the rotation to face forward by count 6. The arm styling — keeping your right arm close to your ear and tracing your body from behind your neck down through count 7 — is what separates a clean turn from a sloppy one. Every movement should be deliberate, not tentative.

mechanics.action: Prep step with rightward body twist; arm begins to lift near right ear
TURN HAPPENS HERE — pivot off right foot, left foot swings left, rotation begins
Break — complete the rotation, land facing forward
Right foot steps back (leader) or forward (follower) — you should be facing forward now
Face forward — right leg goes BACK on 6, not forward. Weight stays centered
Step in place — just shift weight, don't move the foot. Stay on time.

arm_styling.action: Keep arm close to your RIGHT EAR — bend it, keep it controlled. Do not let it drift outward
Arm traces behind your neck — intentional, not tentative
Arm traces DOWN the body — from neck to hip, with full intention
Arm traces back UP the body — complete the full trace cycle

instructor_quotes: On count 6, you should be facing forward again after the left turn. Your right leg goes back on 6, not forward—keep your weight centered.
The turn happens on count 3. Your weight shifts and you pivot, but count 7 stays in place—just shift your weight without moving that foot.
Keep your arm styling close to your right ear on counts 1-2-3. Don't let it drift outward; bend it and keep it controlled near your body.
Trace your body with your arm styling from count 5 (behind your neck) through count 7 (down the body) to count 1 (up). Do this with intention, not tentatively.

techniques.drill: Do the inside turn without a partner. Count out loud: '1-2-PREP-3-TURN-5-6-FACE FORWARD-7-HOLD.' Freeze on count 6 and check: are you facing the mirror? Is your right foot back? Do this 10 times before adding arm styling.
techniques.common_error: Stepping forward on count 6 instead of back, and letting the arm drift away from the ear during the turn. Both errors throw off your balance and timing. The arm should feel like it's glued near your right ear through counts 1-2-3.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross, step, cross — tight, twisted, intentional
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a solo shine (footwork pattern) done in place. The pattern is cross-step-cross: your back foot crosses behind your front foot, you step to the side, then cross again. The key is keeping your back foot CLOSE behind your front foot — you are not passing your front foot, you are staying tight and controlled. Add hip twist for styling: the visual effect of the Suzy Q comes from the hip rotation, not from how wide your legs go. You can prep the Suzy Q by lifting your right leg on counts 5-6-7-1 before starting the pattern.

mechanics.action: Lift right leg — this is the optional prep before starting the Suzy Q pattern
Cross: back foot crosses CLOSE behind front foot — stay tight, don't pass the front foot
Step: step to the side (small step)
Cross: back foot crosses close behind front foot again
Quarter beat — step only on ODD numbers: count 5
Quarter beat — step only on ODD numbers: count 7. These are the core beats.

arm_styling.action: Arms can mirror the hip twist — opposite arm forward as you cross
Arms settle or prep for next move during quarter beats

instructor_quotes: Cross, step, cross—keep your back foot close behind your front foot. Don't pass your front foot; stay tight and controlled.
When doing Suzy Q, twist your hips for styling. This creates the visual effect of crossing without overextending your legs.
You can prep a Suzy Q by lifting your right leg on counts 5-6-7-1 before starting the cross-step-cross pattern.
After Suzy Q (counts 5-6-7-1-2-3), do quarter beats by stepping only on odd numbers: 1 and 3. These are core beats—just the high numbers.

techniques.drill: Stand still and say 'cross-step-cross' out loud while doing the footwork slowly. Check that your back foot never goes past your front foot. Add hip twist only after the footwork feels automatic. Then add the prep lift on 5-6-7-1.
techniques.common_error: Passing the front foot with the crossing foot, making the pattern too wide. This kills the hip styling and throws off your balance. Keep the cross tight — your feet should almost touch.

techniques.name: Cross Body Lead
techniques.tagline: Guide your follow across your body — assertive, compact, clear
techniques.what: The cross body lead (CBL) is the most fundamental partnered move in NY-style salsa. The leader steps forward on 1, then on count 2 adds a subtle hip twist and arm signal to guide the follower across their body. The follower pivots off their right foot while their left foot swings to the left. Leaders: do NOT step into your follow's space — keep a normal forward step and use body language and touch to communicate direction. Keep your arms at shoulder width around their head — compact, not wide. Followers: keep your right elbow down to maintain frame, and pivot cleanly off your right foot.

mechanics.action: Leader steps forward with left foot — normal step, do not invade follow's space
Leader: subtle hip twist, right hand closer to you, left hand closer to follow — signal the cross
Leader steps to the side, creating the lane for the follower to cross through
Follower pivots off right foot, left foot swings left — crossing through the lane
Follower completes the cross, both dancers reestablish connection
Both return to basic step position, connection restored

arm_styling.action: Leader: twist arm subtly — right hand in, left hand out toward follow. Not exaggerated.
Leader: lift left hand up and out to guide follow through. Keep right hand centered.
Arms at shoulder width around follow's head — compact, controlled, not wide

instructor_quotes: When leading a left turn, twist your arm on count 2 subtly—not exaggerated. Bring your right hand closer to you and your left hand closer to your follow.
Leaders: don't step into your follow's space. Keep a normal step forward but add hip twist on count 2 to signal the left turn.
When leading a left turn, keep your right hand centered and lift your left hand up and out. Don't confuse your follow with mixed signals.
Followers: pivot off your right foot while your left foot swings to the left during a left turn. Keep your right elbow down to maintain frame.
Leaders must be assertive with direction and guide. Use body language and touch to show your follow where to go—don't let them guess.
When turning your follow, keep your arms at shoulder width around their head. Don't use wide arms; stay compact and controlled.

techniques.drill: Leaders: practice the CBL with a wall. Step forward on 1, twist on 2, step to the side on 3. Feel the lane you create. Then add a partner and focus only on count 2 — make the signal clear but subtle. Followers: practice the pivot alone — stand on your right foot and swing your left foot to the left on count 5.
techniques.common_error: Leaders stepping INTO the follower's space on count 1, blocking the lane they need to cross through. Also: using wide arms instead of compact shoulder-width arms around the follow's head — this confuses the signal and can hit the follower.

hard_transitions.why: Students often miss the prep entirely because it happens within the basic step — it looks like a basic step but the body twist on count 2 is the signal. If you don't feel the rightward coil loading, you have skipped the prep and the turn will feel forced.

The turn initiates on count 3, which is the THIRD beat of the first set — students often turn too early (on 2) or too late (on 5). The prep twist on 2 must be complete before the pivot begins on 3. Rushing this transition causes the turn to be off-axis.

After the turn, students are often disoriented and lose the count. The Suzy Q starts on count 1 of the next phrase. You must land from the turn, face forward on 6, do the weight-shift-only on 7, and then immediately begin the cross on 1. There is no extra step to recover — you must be ready.

After the quarter beats (stepping only on odd counts 5 and 7), students must return to the full basic step pattern. The rhythm feels different coming out of quarter beats — you are going from sparse stepping back to 6 steps per phrase. Count out loud to stay on time.

techniques.name: Basic Step
techniques.tagline: The foundation of everything — anchor your 3 and your 7
techniques.what: The On2 basic step is an 8-count pattern split into two halves. Counts 1-2-3 travel forward (or lead forward), with count 3 as a planted anchor. Counts 5-6-7 travel back, with count 7 as the second anchor. The key rule: your foot does NOT move on 3 or 7 — these are stationary weight-shifts only. Moving them will cause you to step on your partner.

mechanics.action: Step forward with your left foot (1), then right foot forward (2) — both feet travel.
ANCHOR — keep your foot planted, shift weight only. Do not move this foot.
Step back with your right foot (5), then left foot back (6) — both feet travel.
ANCHOR — keep your foot planted, shift weight only. Do not move this foot.

arm_styling.action: Arms stay relaxed and low, slightly bent at the elbows. No bouncing in the shoulders.
Mirror the forward half — arms stay low and connected, no reaching or lifting.

instructor_quotes: On counts 3 and 7, keep your weight planted and don't move your foot—these are anchor points that stay in place.
Counts 1 and 2 travel forward; count 3 stays in place. Counts 5 and 6 travel back; count 7 stays in place.
If you move your 3 or 7, you'll step on your partner. Keep these anchor points stationary to maintain the connection.
Take small steps and stay aware of your surroundings, especially when dancing in lines.
Don't bounce
Kill the bouncing
Small steps

Students in line attempt the basic step together — the woman in black shorts shows the forward travel on counts 1-2, heels low, small steps.
Full line visible: instructor leads, students follow. Notice the staggered spacing — 'take small steps and stay aware of your surroundings.'

techniques.drill: Stand alone without music. Say aloud: '1-2-ANCHOR, 5-6-ANCHOR.' On each anchor count, press your foot into the floor and shift weight without lifting. Repeat 8 times, then add music at half speed. Focus on keeping your steps small — no more than shoulder-width travel.
techniques.common_error: Lifting or moving the foot on count 3 or 7. Students often take a full step on the anchor counts, which throws off timing and causes collisions with partners. The anchor is a weight shift, not a step.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross in front, pick up your leg, say it as you do it
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a salsa shine (solo footwork) built on a repeating cross-step-cross pattern. The critical rule is that you ALWAYS cross in front of your standing foot — never behind. The verbal pattern 'cross, step, cross' helps you execute it correctly. After each cross, pick up your leg to prepare for the next movement — don't drag your foot. The circular Suzy Q adds a directional rotation, turning to face four walls (bathroom, wall, door, mirror) as you complete each repetition.

mechanics.action: Cross your right foot in FRONT of your left foot — never behind.
Step your left foot out to the side (the 'step' in 'cross-step-cross').
Cross your right foot in FRONT again — pick up your leg after to prepare.
Cross your left foot in FRONT of your right foot to begin the reverse direction.
Step your right foot out to the side.
Cross your left foot in FRONT again — pick up your leg to prepare for the next rep.

arm_styling.action: Arms can swing naturally opposite to the crossing foot, or be held in a relaxed salsa frame. Keep them low — no big gestures.
As you rotate through the four directions, let your arms follow the body's rotation naturally. Don't force them — connection and simplicity.

instructor_quotes: Always cross in front of your foot, whether crossing over left or right—never behind. This is the standard for Suzy Q.
Say the pattern aloud as you move: 'cross, step, cross, cross, step, cross.' Saying it helps you execute it correctly.
Pick up your leg after the cross to prepare for the next step—don't drag your foot.
For circular Suzy Q, think of four directions: bathroom, wall, door, and mirror.
Create smooth curves and circles rather than sharp corners when transitioning between directions in circular Suzy Q.
You can reverse the circular Suzy Q by starting with your left foot and going to the right instead of left.
If you struggle with Suzy Q, practice Suzy Q in isolation before attempting the full combo.
Great dancing is made of connection and simplicity, not complex movements.
cross, step, cross
always in front
circular motion
around the world
smooth and fun

frames.caption: Instructor demonstrates Suzy Q footwork — the cross-step-cross pattern is visible in the foot position. Students observe from the sides.
Students attempt Suzy Q in line — the woman in black shorts shows the cross position, foot clearly in front of the standing foot.
Circular Suzy Q begins — the instructor (holding a conga) calls 'little circular, just a circle, full circle.' Students begin rotating through directions.
Students mid-circular Suzy Q — the line has shifted orientation slightly as dancers rotate through the four directional points (bathroom, wall, door, mirror).
Full-speed Suzy Q in the fog — the woman in black shorts shows the cross position with leg lifted, demonstrating 'pick up your leg after the cross.'
Suzy Q at speed — the man in pink shirt mirrors the woman's cross position. Both show the 'always in front' crossing technique.

techniques.drill: Stand alone. Say aloud 'cross, step, cross' as you do each movement. Do 4 repetitions facing forward (basic Suzy Q). Then add the circular: face your bathroom wall, complete one Suzy Q, rotate to face the side wall, complete one, rotate to face the door, complete one, rotate to face the mirror, complete one. Keep the curves smooth — no sharp corners between directions.
techniques.common_error: Crossing the foot BEHIND the standing foot instead of in front. This is the single most common error and completely changes the look and feel of the move. Also: dragging the foot instead of picking it up after the cross, which kills the rhythm.

techniques.name: Inside Turn (Right Turn)
techniques.tagline: Start on 6, land on 8, keep it low and snatch — don't present
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the right turn or traveling left turn in NY On2) is a partner move where the follower turns to their right under the leader's raised arm. The leader signals the turn by raising their hand on count 1, the follower begins turning on count 2, and the turn completes by count 6-7. The critical timing rule: the follower starts turning on count 6, not before. After the turn, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with 1-2-3. The hand connection stays right-to-right throughout.

mechanics.action: Leader raises hand to signal the turn — arm goes up on count 1 to prepare the follower.
Follower turns to the RIGHT on count 2. Leader guides them to the right.
Follower commits to the turn — start turning on count 6, not before. Don't hesitate.
Keep your 7 AWAY from your partner, not toward them. This creates space.
LAND on count 8 — this is a pause. Don't rush into the next count.
Continue with the basic step after landing. Maintain right-to-right hand hold throughout.

arm_styling.action: Raise your arm LOW — don't reach high. Keep the arm low and grab low to maintain control.
Use your ELBOW to activate the switch, not your hands. Keep your arm straight and use elbow engagement.
Snatch the hand — don't present it slowly. Quick, decisive hand movement prevents the follower from reaching for the wrong hand.

instructor_quotes: Start turning on count 6, not before. Don't hesitate—commit to the turn at 6.
The follower turns to the right on count 2. As the leader, raise your hand on count 1 to signal the turn, and guide them to the right.
Keep your 7 away from your partner, not toward them. This creates space and prevents stepping on each other.
Don't reach high to grab your partner's hand during a turn. Keep your arm low and grab low to maintain control.
Use your elbows to activate the switch, not your hands. Keep your arm straight and use elbow engagement to signal the hand switch.
Don't present your hand slowly—snatch it. Quick, decisive hand movement prevents the follower from reaching for the wrong hand.
After turning on 6, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with counts 1, 2, 3. Don't rush the landing.
Maintain right-to-right hand hold throughout the turn and transition.

frames.caption: Inside turn in progress — the woman in black shorts turns to her right while the man in pink shirt guides with raised arm. Classic inside turn position.
Mid-turn: follower is rotating, leader's arm is up but LOW — demonstrating 'don't reach high, keep your arm low and grab low.'
Turn completion — follower landing, leader maintaining right-to-right connection. The 'land on count 8' pause is visible in the stillness of the frame.
Post-turn basic step resumes — both dancers back in basic step position after the inside turn, demonstrating the transition back to 1-2-3.
Partner work continues — leader guides follower through the inside turn sequence again. Notice the elbow engagement rather than hand-pulling.
Right-to-right hand hold clearly visible as the couple dances — the connection maintained throughout the turn and transition.
Leader's back to camera, follower facing — shows the spatial relationship and the 'keep your 7 away from your partner' principle in action.

techniques.drill: With a partner: practice ONLY the hand raise signal on count 1, then the follower turn on count 2, stopping there. Repeat 8 times until the signal is automatic. Then add the full turn. Focus on the leader keeping the arm LOW and using elbow activation — not hand-pushing. Finally, practice the landing on count 8 by counting aloud: '6-turn, 7-space, 8-LAND, 1-2-3.'
techniques.common_error: Starting the turn too early (before count 6) or rushing through the landing on count 8. Leaders also commonly reach too high with their arm and push with their hand instead of using elbow activation. Followers often reach for the wrong hand because the leader presents slowly instead of snatching.

techniques.name: Transition Back to Basic
techniques.tagline: Land on 8, pause, then flow into 1-2-3
techniques.what: After any turn or shine, returning cleanly to the basic step requires a specific landing protocol. You land on count 8 — this is a deliberate pause, not a rushed step. From that landing, you flow naturally into counts 1-2-3 of the next basic. The right-to-right hand hold is maintained throughout, so there is no hand switch needed. This transition is what makes the combo feel smooth rather than choppy.

mechanics.action: Complete the turn or shine movement — this is the last active count of the previous move.
Keep your 7 away from your partner — create space, don't crowd.
LAND — this is a pause. Plant your foot, absorb the weight, breathe.
Flow into the basic step. Don't rush — let the 8 breathe before you go.

arm_styling.action: Arms settle back to basic frame position during the landing pause.
Resume normal basic step arm position — low, relaxed, connected.

instructor_quotes: After turning on 6, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with counts 1, 2, 3. Don't rush the landing.
Maintain right-to-right hand hold throughout the turn and transition. Don't switch back to the original hand position—keep the connection flowing.
connection and simplicity

frames.caption: The landing moment — both dancers show the count-8 pause position after completing the inside turn. Weight is absorbed, arms are settling.
Transition into basic step — count 1 begins after the count-8 landing. The flow from turn to basic is visible in the body positions.
Basic step resumes fully — the transition is complete. Right-to-right hand hold maintained throughout.

techniques.drill: Practice the transition in isolation: do one inside turn, then FREEZE on count 8 and hold for 2 full seconds. Then step into 1-2-3. Repeat until the pause feels natural rather than forced. The goal is to make the 8 feel like a breath, not a stop.
techniques.common_error: Rushing from the turn directly into count 1 without landing on count 8. This causes the basic step to start on the wrong count and throws off the partnership timing for the rest of the song.

choreography.sequence: BASIC STEP -> SUZY Q (linear) -> CIRCULAR SUZY Q (around the world) -> BASIC STEP -> COMBO (card out + around + anchor) -> INSIDE TURN (right turn) -> TRANSITION BACK TO BASIC -> PARTNER WORK

steps.body: Instructor in black Adidas top faces students. Upright posture, weight centered. Students observe from the sides. The woman in black shorts and man in pink shirt are visible as the primary student group. Instructor holds a conga drum — this is the pre-fog, clear-visibility phase.

Camera angle shifted — now behind the student group. Instructor visible at left demonstrating. Woman in black shorts and man in pink shirt attempt the basic step. Feet show small forward travel on counts 1-2. Audience lines the walls watching.

Instructor introduces Suzy Q. Students in line — woman in black shorts shows cross-in-front position. Foot clearly crossing in front of standing foot, not behind. Instructor calls 'little circular, just a circle.' Conga drums visible in background.
steps.cue: little circular, just a circle, full circle

steps.move: Circular Suzy Q — Around the World
steps.body: Students attempt circular Suzy Q. The line has begun rotating — dancers are turning to face different directions (the four walls). Instructor calls 'around the world.' Woman in black shorts shows the cross position mid-rotation. Man in pink shirt follows.
steps.cue: around the world. We go and 12, 9, 6, basic and 1, 2, 3

steps.body: Circular Suzy Q continues. Students have rotated approximately 90 degrees from starting position. The line is staggered — instructor has called 'small steps.' Woman in black shorts is mid-cross, leg picked up. Man in pink shirt mirrors.
steps.cue: circular and 1, 2, 3, this is for basic and 1, 2, around the world

steps.body: FOG MACHINE ACTIVATES. Visibility drops significantly. Students continue moving — the combo sequence begins. Instructor calls 'combo and card out.' The woman in black shorts and man in pink shirt are the primary visible dancers. Basic step resumes as the combo starting point.
steps.cue: Now we go combo and card out and 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7

steps.body: Full speed Suzy Q in heavy fog. Woman in black shorts shows the cross position clearly — foot in front, leg picked up after the cross. Man in pink shirt is in the step position of the cross-step-cross pattern. Both dancers show good 'always in front' technique.

Suzy Q at speed — both primary dancers show the cross-step-cross pattern simultaneously. The woman's foot is clearly crossing in front. Man in pink shirt mirrors. The fog creates atmospheric effect but footwork is still visible.

Students in basic step — the anchor count (7) is visible in the planted foot position of the woman in black shorts. Weight shifted but foot not moved. Man in pink shirt shows the same anchor. This is the 'keep your weight planted' moment.

Forward travel on counts 1-2. Woman in black shorts steps forward, man in pink shirt steps forward. Both show small steps — no large lunges. The fog is thick but the footwork pattern is clear from the leg positions.

Back travel on counts 5-6. The line of dancers steps back together. Woman in black shorts and man in pink shirt show the backward travel. Fog is at maximum density — dancers are silhouettes but movement is clear.
steps.cue: 6, 7. OK. Can we hold it? 1 more time. 1 right turn.

steps.body: Suzy Q cross position — woman in black shorts shows the cross-in-front clearly. Man in pink shirt is in the step position. The pattern 'cross, step, cross' is visible across the two dancers' positions.

The 'step' in cross-step-cross — woman in black shorts has her foot out to the side (the step between the two crosses). Man in pink shirt is in the cross position. The alternating pattern between the two dancers shows the timing offset.
Basic step forward travel. The line of dancers moves forward together. Woman in black shorts leads the line, man in pink shirt follows. Small steps visible — no bouncing in the upper body.
Basic step back travel. Dancers step back on counts 5-6. The fog has lightened slightly — footwork more visible. Woman in black shorts shows the back step with weight fully transferred.

Suzy Q cross position — the cross-in-front technique is clearly visible. Woman in black shorts has her crossing foot clearly in front of the standing foot. This is the key teaching moment: 'always in front, never behind.'

After the cross — woman in black shorts shows the leg pickup position. The foot is lifted off the floor after the cross, preparing for the next step. This is the 'pick up your leg after the cross — don't drag your foot' teaching point.
steps.cue: Give it up for the ladies!

steps.body: The combo sequence begins — 'card out' position. Woman in black shorts and man in pink shirt show the card-out arm position. This is the transition from basic step into the combo that leads to the inside turn.

The 'around' portion of the combo — woman in black shorts is moving around the man in pink shirt. This is the 'around the world' element within the combo sequence. Both dancers show the spatial relationship of the around movement.

The anchor position within the combo — woman in black shorts plants her foot on count 7. Man in pink shirt shows the anchor on his side. This is the 'anchor the 7' teaching point applied within the combo context.

Inside turn setup — man in pink shirt raises his arm on count 1 to signal the turn. Woman in black shorts is preparing to turn to her right. The arm is LOW — demonstrating 'don't reach high, keep your arm low.'
Follower (woman in black shorts) begins turning to her right on count 6. Leader (man in pink shirt) guides with elbow activation. The turn is just beginning — 'start turning on count 6, not before.'

Mid-turn position — follower is rotating to her right, leader maintains the right-to-right connection. The leader's arm is up but not high — elbow is the activation point. The follower's momentum carries the turn.

Turn nearing completion — follower has rotated approximately 270 degrees. Leader's arm is coming down. The 'keep your 7 away from your partner' principle is visible — there is space between the dancers, not crowding.

The count-8 landing — follower plants her foot and absorbs the weight. This is the deliberate pause before continuing with 1-2-3. Leader is in position, right-to-right connection maintained. 'Land on count 8 — don't rush the landing.'

Transition complete — both dancers resume basic step on count 1 after the count-8 landing. Right-to-right hand hold maintained. The flow from inside turn back to basic is smooth — 'connection and simplicity.'

hard_transitions.note: The circular Suzy Q starts from basic but adds rotation — students often lose the count when adding the turn. The cross-step-cross pattern must stay tight while turning to face each wall.
Around the world is a half-rotation that follows the circular Suzy Q. Students confuse which direction to go because they just finished turning. Anchor on counts 3 and 7 — these feet stay planted.
After rotating moves, students are disoriented and step on wrong counts. Return to basic by finding count 1 and stepping forward (leader) — the anchor on 3 and 7 resets your orientation.
Transitioning from solo shines to partner work requires re-establishing connection. Leaders must be assertive with direction — snatch the hand, dont present it. Keep it low.

drills.name: Solo Basic with Anchors
drills.instructions: Basic step counting out loud. On counts 3 and 7, press your foot into the floor and say "ANCHOR." These are the counts that must never travel.

drills.name: Suzy Q Review
drills.instructions: Cross, step, cross — say it out loud. Crosses ALWAYS in front. Pick up your foot after each cross, dont drag. Add hip twist for styling.

drills.name: Suzy Q to Basic Transition
drills.instructions: Do 2 Suzy Qs then immediately return to basic. The transition is the hard part — find count 1 and step forward cleanly.

sections.name: New Material: Circular Suzy Q + Around the World

drills.name: Circular Suzy Q — 4 Walls
drills.instructions: Cross-step-cross while rotating to face each wall: bathroom, mirror, door, back wall. Create smooth curves, NOT sharp corners. Do 8 full rotations.

drills.name: Around the World
drills.instructions: Half rotation: face front, turn to face back, return to front. Anchor counts 3 and 7 — these feet STAY. Repeat 12x.

drills.name: Combo: Circular Suzy Q (half) + Around the World
drills.instructions: Circular Suzy Q halfway (face 2 walls), then immediately around the world. The anchor on 3 and 7 is what connects them. Repeat 8x.

drills.name: Reverse Direction
drills.instructions: Do the circular Suzy Q to the RIGHT instead of left. Same cross-step-cross, opposite rotation. This feels awkward — thats normal. 8 reps.

drills.name: Walk-Through (No Music)
drills.instructions: Basic -> Circular Suzy Q (half) -> Around the World -> Basic -> Right Turn -> Basic. Count out loud. Get the sequence in your body.

drills.name: Slow Music
drills.instructions: Same combo to a slow salsa track. Focus on smooth transitions — dont rush between moves. Use the breaks between 3s to reset.

drills.name: Full Speed
drills.instructions: Full tempo. If you lose the count, STOP, find 1, restart from basic. Kill the bouncing — stay low and smooth. Remember: connection and simplicity over complexity.
